Date: 2022-08-22
REMARKS
Claims 21, 23-27, 29, 31-37, and 39-50 are pending. Claims 21 and 25 are amended. Support for the claim amendments may be found in the as-filed claims and specification; e.g., at [0008]-[0009]. Claims 1-20, 22, 28, 30, and 38 were previously cancelled. No new matter enters by way of the present amendment. Entry of the amendment and reconsideration of the application based on the following remarks is respectfully requested.
I. Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103
A. Claims 21, 23-26, 29, and 37
The Examiner rejects claims 21, 23-26, 29, and 37 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 for allegedly being unpatentable over US Publication No. 2016/0338591 to Lachenbruch et al.
("Lachenbruch") in view of US Publication No. 2015/0186607 to Geleijnse et al. ("Geleijnse") and further in view of "Capacitive Biosensors" to Berggren ("Berggren"). See Office Action at 5. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that "Lachenbruch et al. teaches a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient at risk of developing pressure ulcers (PU) during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting, the method comprising the steps of: making a plurality of Sub-Epidermal Moisture (SEM) measurements at a body location on the patient at the second care setting. . . each SEM measurement comprising a measurement of biocapacitance... determining whether the delta value exceeds a threshold. . . do nothing if the delta value does not exceed the threshold. . . do something if the delta value exceeds the threshold. " Id. at 5-6. The Examiner concedes that Lachenbruch "does not explicitly teach a current intervention as well as the optionality to change the intervention based on the measurements." Id. at 7. However, the Examiner cites Geleijnse for providing "identifying a current PU intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting... wherein the current PU intervention of level-K is provided in a transfer record... do nothing by continuing to administer the current PU intervention... do something by administering a new PU intervention of level-N, where N has a value greater than K." Id. at 7-8. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to 1) identify a current PU intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting, wherein the current PU intervention of level-K is provided in a transfer record, 2) continue to administer the current PU intervention, and 3) administer a new PU intervention of level-N, where N has a value greater than K as taught by Geleijnse et al. in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al. with the motivation(s) of monitoring a patient's condition and adjusting the level of care accordingly."
Id. at 8. Furthermore, the Examiner cites Berggren for providing "calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements," and concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute 4) calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements as taught by Berggren for the collection of other values as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al. and Geleijnse et al. in combination (more particularly, paragraph [0037] of Lachenbruch et al.) since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. at 8-9.
Applicant respectfully disagrees for at least the reasons already in the record, and further, that the Office has not considered the surprisingly efficacious results as an indicia of non- obviousness.
1. Claimed methods yield unexpected results
Even if assuming arguendo that there is motivation to combine Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, and Berggren to arrive at the pending claims (Applicant does not concede), Applicant submits that the claimed methods for continuity of care provides unexpected benefits, which in turn establishes the non-obviousness of the claimed methods. As the Federal Circuit has repeatedly emphasized, secondary evidence of non-obviousness, including unexpected properties, "may be the most probative and cogent evidence in the record." Apple v. ITC, No. 12-1338 (Fed. Cir. 2013) (citing Transocean Offshore Deepwater Drilling, Inc. v. Maersk, 699 F.3d 1340, 1349 (Fed. Cir. 2012); see also Leo Pharma. Prods., Ltd. v. Rea, 726 F.3d 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2013). Thus, Applicant respectfully asserts that the Examiner has not established aprimafacie case of obviousness, while the unexpected properties that Applicant discovered in the claimed methods are sufficient to overcome any prima facie case of obviousness the Examiner could have raised. See M.P.E.P. § 2145 ("Rebuttal evidence may also include evidence that the claimed invention yields unexpectedly improved properties or properties not present in the prior art.").
The claimed method for continuity of care unexpectedly reduced incidence of PU significantly in acute care settings, to the point of total elimination of PUs. See, e.g., Musa et al., Journal of Wound Care, 30(3): 2-11 (2021) ("Musa"). As described in Musa, patients who were PU-free on admission were scanned daily over discrete anatomical locations as part of the routine skin assessment. Musa at 2. This is equivalent to receiving the lowest level of PU intervention at a first care setting, and providing the level-0 intervention in a transfer record. By implementing the claimed methods in these patients after transfer to a second care setting, Musa determined that health professionals changed their clinical decisions in 40% of the patients who were SEM scanned. Id. at 7. Furthermore, "[c]linical judgement informed by SEM deltas alone, where skin and tissue assessments did not show visible discolouration, resulted in changed health professional clinical decision-making in 82% of patients []." Id. As a result, the claimed method for continuity of care reduced incidence of PU by 87.2% in acute care settings, and as much as 100% at 10 of the 15 test sites. That is, the incidence of PUs was surprisingly completely eliminated. In contrast, "despite the availability of evidence-based best practice guidelines and regional initiatives, . . . [t]he reported prevalence rate has not decreased over the past four years []." Id. at 2.
On the other hand, Lachenbruch, at best, is directed to "alternative systems and methods which provide early indication of a change in tissue status." Lachenbruch at [0005]. Although Lachenbruch seeks to "reduce the development of a pressure ulcer or other tissue breakdown," it does not suggests that its methods are able to reduce incidence of PU by as much as 100%. Id. at [0044]. Similarly, Geleijnse is directed to a "clinical support system and a corresponding clinical support method. . . obtaining current patient data descriptive of a patient, for whom a recommendation for a transition from a current care levels to one or more other care levels shall be provided, in the current care level, obtaining historic patient data of the patient obtained earlier in the current and/or other care levels." Geleijnse at Abstract. Geleijnse provides no indication of pressure ulcer reduction, other than merely to "better assist a clinician to plan resources and to tailor care of a patient." Id. at [0004]. Accordingly, a skilled artisan reading Lachenbruch and Geleijnse, even if they were motivated to combine the references, would not have expected the combination to completely eliminate the incidence of pressure ulcers. The unexpected properties in the claimed methods are sufficient to overcome any prima facie case of obviousness the Examiner could have raised.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 21, 23-26, 29, and 37 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse and further in view of Berggren.
B. Claim 27
The Examiner rejects claim 27 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 for allegedly being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as previously applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 9,028,407 to Bennet-Guerrero ("Bennet- Guerrero"). See Office Action at 14. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Bennet-Guerrero provides "continuing to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold." Id. at 15. As such, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time [] the invention was filed would have found it obvious to continue to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold as taught by Bennett-Guerrero in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination with the motivation(s) of being a way to store and retrieve information from a database." Id. at 15-16. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claim 27 is dependent from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, and Berggren, and Bennet-Guerrero does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claim 27 is also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 27 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as previously applied to claim 21, and further in view of Bennet-Guerrero.
C. Claims 31, 32, 34, and 39

Office Action at 16. Specifically for claim 31, the Examiner alleges that Heaton provides "querying the database for data to form retrieved data values (see FIG. 9 where there is a directory for storing and retrieving archived responses into and from the database. In order for the system here to access the database here, it would query the database in order to retrieve the necessary data)." Id. at 16. As such, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time the invention was filed would have found it obvious to query the database for data to form retrieved delta values as taught by Heaton in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination with the motivation(s) of being a way to store and retrieve information from a database." Id. at 17. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 are dependent directly or indirectly from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, and Berggren, and Heaton does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 are also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as previously applied to claim 29, and further in view of Heaton.
D. Claim 33

Id. at 20. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to 1) create an additional data record, wherein the data element comprises. . . and 2) report the additional data record to the database as taught by Miller et al. in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al. and Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination with the motivation(s) of updating a patient files."
Id. at 20-21. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Rothman provides "the step of analyzing the retrieved values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to-intercept of a selected threshold value." Id. at 21. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time [] the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have the step of analyzing the retrieved values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to-intercept of a selected threshold value as taught by Rothman et al. in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., Berggren, and Heaton in combination with the motivation(s) of alerting a user if a patient is getting better or worse at an accelerating rate." Id. at 22. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 35 and 36 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren, further in view of Heaton as previously applied to claim 32, and further in view of Rothman.
